variants.name: View as a table of function pointers (plain C)
variants.idiom_name: struct of function pointers + opaque context pointer, presenter functions over app state
variants.implementation_notes: Without a library, the classic structure is hand-written: define the view as a struct holding function pointers (set_title, get_query, ...) plus an opaque context pointer, let each screen fill that table with its widget code, and write the presenter as ordinary functions over a shared application-state struct that call through the table. The view remains a pure sink: it never dereferences the model, and the presenter is the only code that touches both sides. This is the replacement for the class/interface form C does not have; the classic structure stays justified wherever a screen has real presentation logic, but a trivial dialog is better served by direct widget code.
pitfalls: The function table carries no lifetime: the view struct and its ctx must outlive every presenter call, and a screen freed without clearing the table leaves dangling function pointers - C has no vtable reload.
A view that also writes model state re-creates the coupling the pattern removes; keep model mutation inside presenter functions and document it.
NULL entries are the C substitute for an unimplemented interface method - decide once whether a missing method is a no-op or aborts, and keep that rule in one place.

variants.name: GObject interface + signals (GLib/GTK)
variants.idiom_name: GTypeInterface with vfuncs + g_signal_connect notifications on a GObject view
variants.implementation_notes: When GLib is already linked, GObject supplies the object machinery C lacks: register the view as a GTypeInterface whose vfuncs are the view contract, have the screen's GObject type implement it, and use the signal system (g_signal_connect on the view's widget signals, g_signal_emit for presenter-driven notifications) instead of hand-wired callbacks. The presenter is then a plain object or module that receives the interface pointer - or a GObject itself when it needs properties. Choose this over the function-pointer table when the project already uses GTK/GLib and wants introspection, signals and cross-language bindings; the plain table stays the better fit for freestanding or embedded C without GLib.
pitfalls: GObject interfaces are runtime-registered types: a missing prerequisite or an interface added after the type is instantiated fails at runtime with a GLib critical, not at compile time.

Signal handlers are synchronous and the connection owns a reference to the data pointer only if you pass a destroy notify; forgetting g_signal_handler_disconnect or the destroy notify keeps the presenter alive.
The vfunc table is filled by interface init, so the implementing type must cast correctly (G_TYPE_CHECK_INSTANCE_CAST-style macros) or the vfunc pointer is garbage.
